Vice President Han Zheng did not mention the US by name in his remarks. The US has launched a pressure campaign on Cuba that has largely blocked oil from reaching the island. The US war on Iran started with US-Israeli strikes in February.

"China holds that the sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East, including the Gulf, should be respected."

Amnesty International says defendants were tortured into giving 'confessions' later used as evidence, as 50 more face death
Libyan military commander Khalifa Haftar leaves after talks with Greece's foreign minister in Athens, on 17 January 2020 (Aris Messinis/AFP)
Off
At least 30 men have been executed in eastern Libya since late August after being sentenced to death in secretive military trials and at least 50 others remain at imminent risk of execution, local media and rights groups have reported over the last week.
Amnesty International said the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), led by eastern commander Khalifa Haftar and the de facto authorities in the region, resumed executions on 23 August in Libya for the first time since 2010.
Those executed had been convicted following “grossly unfair and secretive trials” marred by torture, the rights group said.
Some of those executed or still awaiting death sentences were convicted of murder and terrorism-related offences linked to fighting between the LAAF and opposing armed groups between 2014 and 2018, Amnesty said.
Several detainees claimed to have been tortured by armed groups affiliated with the LAAF following their arrests, including to obtain “confessions” that were later used as evidence against them, the rights group said.
“The LAAF authorities must immediately halt all executions,” the organisation said, calling for a moratorium and the overturning of convictions and death sentences handed down following unfair trials.
Amnesty also called on authorities to retry civilians accused of internationally recognised criminal offences in accordance with international standards of fairness in civilian courts that do not use evidence obtained through torture.
It called on authorities to grant international monitors access to Gernada and other detention sites in eastern Libya.

Harold's nobility is framed by his hunting with falcons, a symbol of authority originating in Sassanid royal art (Wikimedia Commons)
Off
The Bayeux Tapestry reflects a hidden heritage of trade networks that extended well beyond Europe into the Islamic world, showcasing the migration of Islam's sophisticated artistic motifs.
Islamic aesthetic choices were stitched into the borders of an English historic chronicle, heavily shaping the visual identity of Norman royalty. The clearest evidence can be seen in the borders that frame it, top and bottom, inhabited by hundreds of animals. None of them is random. All were chosen specifically for their meanings, many derived from eastern sources.
Medieval monastic scriptoriums kept visual archives of foreign designs, ensuring that highly complex Islamic and Sassanid silk patterns could be preserved and reproduced across generations. The actual silk fabrics themselves were incredibly expensive luxury items, so monks and master illuminators deconstructed, catalogued and stored these motifs through the creation of pattern books (Musterbucher).
When a high-status Islamic textile arrived at a monastery, usually as a diplomatic gift, a wrap for holy relics, or a royal vestment, a master artist would carefully sketch the pattern into the monastery's pattern books. These were specialised, pocket-sized reference manuals filled entirely with sketches, animal figures, scrolling border layouts and alphabet styles.

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said the declining public support for Israel in the United States was due to a lack of “biblical literacy”, disinformation and hostility towards people who believe in God.
Huckabee told NewsNation in an interview on Thursday that there were “three sources” behind what he called the erosion of support for Israel.
He cited foreign propaganda and disinformation, hatred of people who believe “there is a God and that he’s made up the rules for life” and a lack of knowledge of the Bible.

Huckabee also dismissed claims that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza and that it is an apartheid state, saying Americans would have a more favourable view of Israel if they would “look at the truth”.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne leave a press conference on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, 14 April 2026 (Andrej Ivanov/AFP)
Off
A Canadian Liberal Party lawmaker has said he was removed from his position as parliamentary secretary to the minister of veterans affairs after backing legislation aimed at regulating the country's arms exports to Israel.
Sean Casey, who represents Charlottetown in Prince Edward Island, told CBC News a Liberal whip warned him in March that supporting New Democratic Party lawmaker Jenny Kwan’s private member’s bill would mean his removal from the parliamentary secretary post.
The bill was reportedly meant to close a loophole that allows Canadian-made military equipment to be exported to another country and then end up in Israel.
Casey said he supported the measure because of concerns raised by voters in his riding, although the bill was defeated in the House of Commons.
Casey was the only one of the 15 Liberal MPs to vote for the bill, and the only one of them in a position as a parliamentary secretary.
He said he was told of his removal during a call from the prime minister’s office on Thursday and was replaced by Quebec MP Sophie Chatel a day later.
Kwan, who tabled the bill, said the episode was troubling and asked whether Liberal MPs were really free to vote as their constituents wanted.
“A Parliamentary Secretary should not have to choose between doing their job and following their conscience,” Kwan said in a statement on her website.
The government may oppose her bill, she added, but MPs “should not have to fear losing their parliamentary responsibilities simply for voting according to their conscience”.

Just a year ago, the conference was overshadowed by speculation that Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, could challenge Keir Starmer for the Labour leadership.
It didn't happen then, but months later, Starmer resigned - turning this year's conference into a very different affair.
Burnham's arrival as the premier has injected new energy and hope into the Labour membership, as well as the parliamentary party itself.
Polling shows that Labour is starting to regain some of the voters who had abandoned it in droves under Starmer for Reform UK on the right and the Green Party on the left.
The figures suggest Labour would be the largest party if a general election was held tomorrow, but may still fall short of a majority.
All eyes are on Burnham to use the conference to unveil a bold and comprehensive new vision for the government.
The four-day gathering will bring Labour MPs, councillors, activists and members to Liverpool, alongside trade unionists, business leaders and NGO representatives, and is expected to dominate the news cycle in Britain until Wednesday.
So far Burnham's government has mainly introduced small but popular policies. He has also set up a No 10 North in Manchester, a second seat of government, as part of a drive towards regional rebalancing.
But the country is still yet to see how radically different - or not - the Burnham premiership will turn out to be from Starmer's. This conference will be the key moment.

Submitted by

Black and Arab communities in France confront deep‑rooted prejudices when they venture into outdoor sports. But the 'we're coming' movement is pushing back
People sit beside a lake above L'Alpe d’Huez in the French Alps, 23 August 2023 (Jeff Pachoud/AFP)
Off
It all began with a video posted on TikTok in August, where the author celebrated the absence of ethnically diverse hikers in the mountains and claimed the space as one exclusively reserved for white people.
“One of the rare places in France without Wallah and Gucci caps, where you can feel safe,” he wrote over a breathtaking Alpine landscape, using an interjection meaning “by God” in Arabic that has passed into French slang.
The video, now deleted, triggered two types of reaction on social media.
First came a wave of racist and Islamophobic insults, arguing for the confinement of people from the banlieues – France’s working‑class, often ethnically diverse suburbs – to their neighbourhoods. Comments such as “stay where you belong, in your Islamised districts” were rife, along with accusations of a lack of civility, such as: “Nature must stay clean. No peeing, no trash, no animal‑like screaming.”
Then came an unexpected counterattack that became a viral trend, both humorous and political, rallying around the slogan “Wallah, we’re coming”.
Young people, alone or in groups, women wearing hijab, families – all posed in forests, on mountain peaks, on horseback, or while trekking and hiking, to announce their presence in spaces where they consider themselves fully legitimate.
Among them was Zeynab Alabbar, co‑founder and creative director of Kamak, a modest sportswear brand. She joined the movement by filming herself and friends scrambling up shaded trails or admiring the scenery.

UAE-owned Manchester City found guilty of financial rules breach, report says
The UAE-owned Manchester City have been found guilty on all but one of the 115 financial charges it faces for breaching financial rules, the Athletic reported, an outcome that could send shockwaves through English soccer and potentially sour UAE-UK relations.
City was charged by the Premier League in 2023 following an investigation into alleged breaches between 2009 and 2018.
It was accused of failing to provide accurate financial information and details of payments to players and coaches, as well as breaches of financial sustainability rules.
According to the Athletic, no sanction had yet been decided and City is set to appeal. But the BBC reported that the punishment decided by the panel will be released before any appeal is completed.
If found guilty, City are looking at a points deduction serious enough to relegate them, large fines or, in the worst-case scenario, even expulsion from the Premier League.
Read more: UAE-owned Manchester City found guilty of financial rules breach, report says
Under the ownership of Sheikh Mansour, City have become the dominant force in English football. (AFP)

Morning recap
Good morning, Middle East Eye readers.
If you're just joining us, here are key developments:
• Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran had presented the United States with a “concrete” seven-day plan and that the choice now rested with Washington.
• The United States is having positive, constructive discussions with Iran through mediators and continues to discuss nuclear issues, a US official said on Friday when asked about Iran's proposed seven-day plan.
• Oman’s Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi and his Iranian counterpart Araghchi have discussed regional developments and efforts to ensure safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
• US President Trump has rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day ceasefire and has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms, The Wall Street Journal reported.
• Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said that his country would allow UN nuclear inspectors into the country.
• The Saudi Arabia-led coalition forces in Yemen said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom.
• Yemen's government forces say they have made advances in the southern Taiz governorate, taking control of several areas and higher ground, according to Al Jazeera.
• The United Nations human rights office issued a list on Friday adding 61 more companies operating in Israeli-occupied West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.
• Deputy prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, Nazhat Shameem Khan, has said that the court has insulated itself against potential court-wide sanctions from the US, according to the Financial Times.
• Six Palestinians were arrested by Israeli forces across the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
• Forty-one US lawmakers have called on Secretary of State Mark Rubio to press Israel for the release of Palestinian healthcare workers.

after.author: Hilal Saki
after.summary:
UN expands list of companies operating in West Bank settlements
The United Nations human rights office issued a list on Friday adding 61 more companies operating in Israeli West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.
The database is highly sensitive as firms could be targeted for boycotts or divestment to pressure Israel over settler expansion in the territory that is home to over three million Palestinians.
The database, first released in 2020, now includes 214 firms, mostly from Israel, but also from 10 other countries including France, Germany, China and the US.
Newly added firms included Israeli pesticides maker ADAMA, part of Chinese-owned Syngenta Group, Israel-based real estate investment holding company Alony Hetz and Spain's Salvat Logistica.
They did not immediately respond to a request for comment on their inclusion in the UN database.
They joined companies such as travel agency Expedia and home-rental company Airbnb already on the list.
Report by Reuters
